children: Port employers in Southern California and unionized security guards reached a tentative labor deal, averting a strike threat at the nation's busiest container-handling complex as retailers rush in last-minute holiday items.

The Pacific Maritime Association said early Saturday the current labor contract with 250 guards at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach would be extended pending ratification of the tentative deal by the workers.

The contract with the local chapter of the International Longshore and Warehouse Union had been due to expire at 12:01 a.m. Saturday and the guards had already voted to authorize a strike. Although the guards account for just 2% of the ports' unionized workforce, other ILWU dockworkers were expected to refuse to cross picket lines.

"This agreement provides certainty for the ports, for the cargo owners and workers throughout the supply chain who depend on them, and for the Southern California, regional and national economies," the employers said in a statement.
Union representatives didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Southern California ports have been deluged with cargo this fall. In October, the ports moved a combined more than 1 million loaded import boxes, measured in 20-foot-equivalent units, for the second month in a row as the traditional peak shipping season extended into the final quarter of the year.
Shipping industry officials had warned that a strike would affect six of the ports' 13 container-handling terminals, accounting for more than half of the gateway's cargo.

Port employers warned this week of growing potential for a strike because of a lack of progress in labor talks. The maritime association said earlier this week that its contract offer included a pay increase that would lift average full-time wages to $198,000 from more than $170,000.
The employers didn't provide details of the wage offer in the tentative deal.
